content.title: KITCHEN MISTAKES THAT TURN YOUR {{FOOD}} DANGEROUS
facts: **Cantaloupe – Don't leave cut melon out for hours (bacteria like Listeria grow fast on its moist surface).**
**Ground meat – Don't thaw it on the counter (outer layer sits in the bacteria danger zone long before the center defrosts).**
**Garlic in oil – Don't store homemade garlic-oil at room temperature (low-oxygen environment can let Clostridium botulinum grow).**
**Chicken – Don't rinse it under the tap before cooking (splashing water spreads bacteria across your sink and counters).**
**Leftover rice-based dishes – Don't cool them slowly on the stove (bacteria multiply fastest in the first hours after cooking).**
**Raw sprouts – Don't eat them uncooked if you're pregnant or immunocompromised (warm, humid growing conditions make them a common Salmonella source).**
**Soft cheeses – Don't store them next to ready-to-eat foods without wrapping (Listeria can transfer easily in the fridge).**
**Eggs – Don't store them on the fridge door (temperature swings there speed up bacterial growth through the shell).**

caption:
A few of these mix-ups are way more common than people think. Take cantaloupe: its rough, netted skin traps bacteria, and once it's cut, that bacteria has direct access to the moist flesh — sitting out even a couple hours at room temperature gives it the perfect window to multiply. Ground meat is another sneaky one: because it's processed from multiple cuts, bacteria gets mixed throughout the meat instead of staying on the surface, so thawing it slowly and unevenly on the counter lets that bacteria build up before the inside ever reaches a safe temperature. And garlic-in-oil is a classic home-cooking trap — garlic is low-acid and oil blocks oxygen, which is exactly the environment Clostridium botulinum spores need to wake up and produce toxin, something heat from cooking won't fix once it's bottled and left unrefrigerated.
